description: I'm doing this solo, too busy to work in a team. But excited to learn all about flames in freefall :)
summary: Pharos is an interactive field guide to fire beyond Earth, built from all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) archive. It opens on an illustrated dinner date that moves to a lunar habitat and asks what the couple would need to consider before lighting the candles: the air, the materials and the unknowns. Explore a labeled candle illustration, search studies by their research questions, read NASA's words and inspect its original tables. Research tools map the archive against the challenge's Moon-base atmosphere and explain the limits: only 20 of 746 table rows with both ambient oxygen and pressure reach the target, all from one cool-flame gas study. None establishes material flammability there. Adjustable research-priority weights, sourced interpretations and visible archive inconsistencies help users decide where to look next. This matters because NASA expects Moon bases to run at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less, making materials much more flammable. Pharos shows what NASA already knows about that regime and where the evidence runs out. Each investigation retains its DOI; the illustration is never data.
details:
Pharos turns NASA's combustion archive into something a habitat designer can actually use. Behind the dinner scene, each of the room's three topics opens part of the evidence. The air leads to a flame lab, where sliders for gravity, oxygen and airflow change a WebGL candle illustration and every behaviour links to the source that describes it. The materials lead to BASS-II, NASA's study of burning and suppressing solids. The unknowns lead to what PSI cannot yet answer.

NASA's archive, in Pharos, replaces 24 records, 22 data tables and hundreds of publication listings with one catalog. Each investigation opens a dossier with NASA's own objective and impacts, its original tables and its DOI. The research tools plot every table row that records both oxygen and pressure, set NASA's verbatim text beside my inference, and let you reweight research priorities, labelled as judgment rather than a risk score. A designer can see which conditions have actually been tested; a researcher can see which experiments are still missing, partial-gravity combustion above all.

I built Pharos solo, through the Chicago local event, directing and reviewing AI coding agents (Claude and Codex) that wrote much of the code. It uses TypeScript, React, WebGL and d3, with Python to parse the PSI data and scripts that recompute every number on screen from the saved files. It ships as static files with no server, accounts or outside requests, so nothing can break or drift during judging.

The creative bet was to start with candles at dinner instead of a table: the blue lunar flame asks the question before any chart does. The constraint I held hardest was honesty. With one person and a deadline, I cut features, never accuracy. Illustrations, estimates and my own judgment are labelled, every count is defined, and every investigation is cited by its DOI.
